correctness.rationale: An elementary first-exceedance argument forces pi_1>=n-m; reverse-complementation forces pi_n<=m+1. The wrap edge then requires n<=3m+1. For m>=2 an explicit decreasing-with-two-moved-endpoints permutation works for every n<=3m+1, including empty-run boundaries. The equality of the bounds at n=3m+1 forces endpoints, then the first-exceedance predecessor argument forces pi_2=n and, by reverse-complement, pi_(n-1)=1. The m=1 path graph has no Hamiltonian cycle for n>=3. Exact finite independent exhaustive checks corroborate all corner cases but are not substitutes for the proof.

evidence: Vella (2003), pp. 3-5, makes the domain cyclic in the *pattern-occurrence definition* and treats rotational equivalence classes, without a numerical adjacent-difference bound.
Domagalski et al. (2021), Introduction and Theorem 2.1, define cyclic pattern containment via some rotation and establish a cyclic Erdős–Szekeres analogue, but impose no bounded numerical jumps.
Nadler (2026), Theorem 1, proves reverse-diagonal localization; even this stronger position bound supplies only the *necessary* cyclic threshold without construction.
broader_coverage.reasoning: General cyclic pattern-avoidance theorems concern a different requirement (all rotations) and do not imply existence of one anchored linear 123-avoiding tour with bounded return jump. Linear localization has been explicitly factored out of the novelty claim.

value.rationale: The new condition of *closing* the bounded-jump tour changes an indefinitely extensible fixed-radius Hamiltonian-path family into a finite-support family. Its exact sharp cutoff n=3m+1, uniformly explicit witnesses, exact optimal jump bandwidth for all n, and forced extremal endpoints form a natural complete bottleneck-feasibility theorem, motivated directly by the source's Hamiltonian-path model. This is not a parameter substitution into the existing linear enumeration, nor merely a finite census.
